questions.stem: A 58 year old man collapses suddenly while queuing in a supermarket. A nurse who is shopping reaches him within a minute. He does not respond to voice or a firm shoulder shake. His lips are blue. He takes an occasional noisy gasp roughly every 15 seconds. No carotid pulse can be felt after 10 seconds.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sudden collapse, unresponsiveness, absent normal breathing (only agonal gasps) and no pulse is cardiac arrest: sudden cessation of cardiac output. Start CPR immediately.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.
Unresponsive, **not breathing normally** (agonal gasps), **no pulse**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: This triad = **cardiac arrest**: start CPR.

elim: Rhythmic jerking with a pulse; he is pulseless.
Causes reduced consciousness but the pulse is preserved.
Focal deficit with a preserved pulse and breathing.
Brief collapse with a pulse and rapid recovery.

steps.x: **A. Cardiac arrest.** Unresponsive + not breathing normally + no pulse = cardiac arrest, start CPR.

questions.stem: An 86 year old woman is found unresponsive on the ward. She has no pulse and is not breathing, and CPR is started. The defibrillator pads are attached. The monitor (see item resources) shows a flat line in two leads with the gain turned up, with no P waves and no QRS complexes.

visual.title: Monitor rhythm
visual.caption: Flat trace with no P waves or QRS complexes: asystole.

questions.q: Which is the most likely rhythm?
questions.e: A flat line confirmed in more than one lead at increased gain, with no electrical activity, is asystole: a non-shockable rhythm.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.

clues: flat line in two leads with the gain turned up
no P waves and no QRS complexes
steps.x: A **flat line**, confirmed in two leads at high gain.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Asystole**: non-shockable.

elim: Shows P waves and slow escape QRS complexes, with a pulse.
Shows organised QRS complexes without a pulse.
A fast broad-complex rhythm.
A chaotic, irregular trace, not a flat line confirmed at high gain.

steps.x: **A. Asystole.** Asystole and PEA are non-shockable; VF and pulseless VT are shockable.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man has a cardiac arrest in the Emergency Department. CPR is in progress. At the rhythm check the monitor (see item resources) shows a regular narrow-complex rhythm at 150 per minute. No central pulse can be felt during a 10 second check.

visual.title: Monitor rhythm
visual.caption: Organised narrow-complex rhythm at 150 per minute; no pulse was palpable: PEA.

questions.q: Which is the most appropriate description of this rhythm for the ALS algorithm?
questions.e: An organised rhythm on the monitor (even one that looks like SVT) with no palpable pulse is pulseless electrical activity, which is non-shockable.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.

clues: regular narrow-complex rhythm at 150 per minute
steps.x: Organised narrow complexes but **no pulse**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **PEA**: non-shockable; look for the 4H/4T cause.

elim: There are clear QRS complexes.
There is no pulse, so it is not perfusing.
The complexes are narrow, not broad.
The rhythm is organised, not chaotic.

steps.x: **B. Non-shockable: pulseless electrical activity.** Organised rhythm + no pulse = PEA, never shock it.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman is brought to the Emergency Department after taking 50 amitriptyline tablets. She becomes unresponsive and pulseless and CPR is started. Before arrest her ECG showed a broad QRS of 160 ms and her pulse rate was 140 bpm. Her glucose, potassium and temperature are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reversible cause of the arrest?
questions.e: Drug overdose (here a tricyclic, which blocks sodium channels and widens the QRS) is a recognised precipitant of cardiac arrest: the 'toxins' T of the 4Ts.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.
**Tricyclic overdose** with a broad QRS; other causes excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: 4Ts: **toxins**.

elim: Potassium is normal.
Her temperature is normal.
No chest trauma or surgery to suggest it.
No features of PE or MI.

steps.x: **E. Toxins.** Drug overdose is a reversible cause: toxins (one of the 4Ts).

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman has had 4 days of profuse vomiting and diarrhoea. She takes bendroflumethiazide and furosemide. She collapses on the ward and is in cardiac arrest with ventricular fibrillation. A blood gas taken during CPR is shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reversible cause of the arrest?
questions.e: Diuretics plus vomiting and diarrhoea have caused severe hypokalaemia, an electrolyte disturbance that can precipitate VF arrest: one of the 4Hs.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.
GI losses on two diuretics; potassium **1.9**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: 4Hs: **hypokalaemia**.

elim: Her potassium is low, not high.
No exposure and nothing suggests a low core temperature.
Not suggested by the history.
No trauma or ventilation to suggest it.

steps.x: **B. Hypokalaemia.** Hypo/hyperkalaemia is one of the 4Hs; check potassium on a gas during CPR.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man with angina has central chest pain while walking his dog and then collapses in the park. A bystander starts CPR and paramedics arrive 6 minutes later. He is unresponsive and pulseless. The defibrillator pads are being attached. He has no history of trauma or overdose.
questions.q: Which is the most likely initial rhythm?
questions.e: VF is the most common initial rhythm in sudden cardiac arrest, especially from ischaemic heart disease.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.
Ischaemic chest pain, then sudden collapse.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Commonest initial rhythm: **VF**.

elim: Usually a later, end-stage rhythm.
He is pulseless, and CHB usually has a pulse.
Usually from a reversible cause such as hypovolaemia; less common initially here.
He has no pulse.

steps.x: **E. Ventricular fibrillation.** Sudden cardiac arrest from IHD: VF is the commonest initial rhythm.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man collapses at a bus stop. A bystander calls for help but says he is 'still breathing' because he makes a snoring gasp every 10 to 20 seconds. He is unresponsive, his chest does not otherwise move and no pulse can be felt.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his breathing pattern?
questions.e: Occasional gasps in an unresponsive, pulseless patient are agonal breathing, not normal breathing. They should trigger immediate recognition of cardiac arrest and CPR.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.
Unresponsive and pulseless with **occasional gasps**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Agonal breathing**: this is cardiac arrest, start CPR.

elim: A waxing and waning pattern with a pulse.
Deep, rapid breathing of metabolic acidosis with a pulse.
A faint has a pulse and normal breathing.
Follows a seizure, with a pulse.

steps.x: **A. Agonal gasps of cardiac arrest.** Agonal gasps are not breathing: start CPR.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man is 4 hours after cardiac bypass surgery. His chest drain output has suddenly stopped. His BP has been falling and his JVP is raised. He then becomes pulseless with sinus rhythm at 110 per minute on the monitor. His chest is moving equally and the trachea is central.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reversible cause of the arrest?
questions.e: PEA after cardiac surgery with a blocked chest drain, falling BP and raised JVP is cardiac tamponade, one of the 4Ts, and needs urgent decompression.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.

clues: chest drain output has suddenly stopped
steps.x: Post-cardiac surgery, **blocked drain**, **raised JVP**, PEA.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: 4Ts: **tamponade**.

elim: Nothing suggests a low core temperature.
The JVP is raised, not low.
The trachea is central and the chest moves equally.
Possible after surgery, but a stopped drain and raised JVP after cardiac surgery point to tamponade.

steps.x: **A. Cardiac tamponade.** PEA usually has a reversible cause; after cardiac surgery think tamponade.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man with alcohol-related liver disease vomits large amounts of fresh blood on the ward. His pulse rate rises to 140 bpm and BP falls to 70/40 mmHg. He then becomes unresponsive and pulseless. The monitor shows sinus tachycardia at 130 per minute.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reversible cause of the arrest?
questions.e: Massive haematemesis has caused PEA from hypovolaemia, one of the 4Hs. Shocks will not help; give blood and fluids while continuing CPR.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.

clues: vomits large amounts of fresh blood
steps.x: Massive bleed, then **PEA**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: 4Hs: **hypovolaemia**.

elim: Not the primary problem; he has lost a large volume of blood.
No surgery, trauma or raised JVP.
No trauma or ventilation.
No overdose history.

steps.x: **A. Hypovolaemia.** PEA from bleeding = hypovolaemia: fluids and blood, not shocks.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has a cardiac arrest on a surgical ward. High-quality CPR is underway and the monitor shows PEA. Adrenaline 1 mg IV has been given. The team leader asks what the team should now prioritise.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate priority?
o: Search for and treat a reversible cause (4Hs and 4Ts)
Stop CPR to recheck the pulse every 30 seconds
questions.e: Once CPR is underway, the priority is to search for and treat a reversible cause using the 4Hs and 4Ts, especially in PEA.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide which test answers the exact question asked (initial or diagnostic).

clues: Adrenaline 1 mg IV has been given
steps.x: CPR running, adrenaline given, **PEA**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Now find the cause: **4Hs and 4Ts**.

elim: Delays CPR; it is not the priority.
PEA is non-shockable.
For shock-refractory VF or pulseless VT only.
Rhythm checks are every 2 minutes; frequent pauses harm perfusion.

steps.x: **D. Search for and treat a reversible cause (4Hs and 4Ts).** 4Hs: hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hypo/hyperkalaemia, hypothermia. 4Ts: tension pneumothorax, toxins, tamponade, thrombosis.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man is pulled from a river in January after 30 minutes in the water. He is pulseless and CPR is started. The monitor shows ventricular fibrillation. His skin is very cold to touch. He has no visible injuries.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the reversible cause?
o: Core temperature with a low-reading thermometer
Tympanic temperature with a standard thermometer
questions.e: Hypothermia is one of the 4Hs. A core temperature with a low-reading thermometer confirms it and changes management (rewarming, adjusted drug and shock strategy).

steps.x: An investigation question: decide which test answers the exact question asked (initial or diagnostic).
Cold-water immersion in winter: **hypothermia**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Measure **core temperature** with a low-reading thermometer.

elim: Not a reversible cause test during CPR.
Does not change resuscitation.
Nothing suggests overdose.
A standard thermometer may not read low enough.

steps.x: **A. Core temperature with a low-reading thermometer.** Hypothermia (a 4H): measure core temperature.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman with severe asthma has a 2 day history of worsening wheeze. In the Emergency Department she becomes exhausted and her chest goes silent. Her oxygen saturation falls to 72% breathing oxygen and she then arrests. The monitor shows PEA. Air entry is equal on both sides and the trachea is central.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reversible cause of the arrest?
questions.e: Life-threatening asthma with a silent chest and saturations of 72% has caused a hypoxic arrest. Hypoxia (a 4H) is treated with airway management and 100% oxygen.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.

clues: Air entry is equal on both sides
steps.x: Silent chest, sats 72%, then PEA; no pneumothorax.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: 4Hs: **hypoxia**.

elim: No exposure; nothing suggests a low temperature.
No blood or fluid loss.
Air entry is equal and the trachea is central.
No overdose history.

steps.x: **C. Hypoxia.** Asthma arrest: think hypoxia (and exclude tension pneumothorax).

questions.stem: A 57 year old man has crushing central chest pain for 40 minutes. His ECG shows ST elevation in V1 to V4. While waiting for transfer to the catheter lab he collapses and is pulseless with ventricular fibrillation. He receives three shocks and has return of spontaneous circulation.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reversible cause of the arrest?
questions.e: An anterior STEMI is coronary thrombosis, one of the 4Ts, and a common precipitant of VF arrest. After ROSC he needs urgent PCI to treat the cause.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide which test answers the exact question asked (initial or diagnostic).

clues: ST elevation in V1 to V4
steps.x: STEMI then VF arrest.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: 4Ts: **thrombosis (coronary)**: treat with PCI.

elim: No exposure.
No blood or fluid loss.
No trauma or surgery.
No overdose history.

steps.x: **D. Thrombosis (coronary).** Thrombosis (PE or MI) is one of the 4Ts; MI is the classic cause of VF arrest.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man collapses in the street. A passer-by finds that he is unresponsive and not breathing normally. There is no defibrillator in sight. A second bystander is nearby. The scene is safe.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial action?
o: Call 999 and start CPR at 30 compressions to 2 breaths
Give 5 rescue breaths and then check for a pulse
Place him in the recovery position
Start CPR at 15 compressions to 2 breaths
Wait for the ambulance before touching him
questions.e: In an adult who is unresponsive and not breathing normally: call for help (999) and start CPR without delay at 30 compressions to 2 breaths.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.

clues: There is no defibrillator in sight
steps.x: Unresponsive, not breathing normally: arrest.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Call 999 and start CPR 30:2**.

elim: That is the paediatric sequence; adults start with compressions.
For an unconscious patient who IS breathing normally.
Adult ratio is 30:2.
Delaying CPR worsens survival.

steps.x: **A. Call 999 and start CPR at 30 compressions to 2 breaths.** Adult BLS: call 999, start CPR 30:2 immediately.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman has a cardiac arrest in a GP surgery. A healthcare assistant starts chest compressions while a colleague fetches the defibrillator. The GP watches and notices that the compressions are slow and shallow. The GP corrects the technique.
questions.q: Which is the correct compression rate and depth?
o: 100 to 120 per minute, 2 to 3 cm deep
100 to 120 per minute, 5 to 6 cm deep
140 to 160 per minute, 7 to 8 cm deep
60 to 80 per minute, 2 to 3 cm deep
80 to 100 per minute, 3 to 4 cm deep
questions.e: Adult compressions are 100 to 120 per minute at a depth of 5 to 6 cm. Early high-quality compressions matter more than any drug.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.
Compressions are too slow and shallow.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Correct: **100 to 120/min, 5 to 6 cm**.

elim: Right rate but too shallow.
Too fast to allow refilling and too deep (risk of injury).
Too slow and too shallow to perfuse.
Too slow and too shallow.

steps.x: **B. 100 to 120 per minute, 5 to 6 cm deep.** CPR: 30:2, 100 to 120 per minute, 5 to 6 cm deep.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man is found pulseless on the cardiology ward. CPR is started and the arrest team escalates to the Advanced Life Support algorithm. Pads are attached and the monitor shows a regular broad-complex tachycardia at 200 per minute with no pulse. An unsynchronised 200 J shock is delivered.

visual.title: Monitor rhythm
visual.caption: Regular broad-complex tachycardia with no pulse: pulseless VT (shockable).

questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate next step?
o: Check for a pulse immediately after the shock
Give adrenaline 1 mg IV before resuming CPR
questions.e: Pulseless VT, like VF, is shockable. After a 200 J unsynchronised shock, CPR resumes immediately and the rhythm is reassessed every 2 minutes.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.

clues: regular broad-complex tachycardia at 200 per minute with no pulse
steps.x: Pulseless VT, shock just given.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Back on the chest at once**; reassess in 2 minutes.

elim: Pausing delays compressions; restart CPR and reassess at 2 minutes.
In shockable rhythms adrenaline is given after the 3rd shock, once compressions have restarted.
Never used in arrest.
Pulseless VT needs unsynchronised defibrillation.

steps.x: **D. Resume CPR immediately for 2 minutes.** Shock, then CPR straight away, rhythm check every 2 minutes.

questions.stem: A 77 year old woman has a cardiac arrest on a care of the elderly ward. CPR at 30:2 is in progress. The monitor shows organised complexes at 60 per minute but there is no pulse. IV access has been obtained. No drugs have been given yet.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Continue CPR and give adrenaline 1 mg IV now
Continue CPR and give adrenaline after 3 cycles
Continue CPR and give amiodarone 300 mg IV
questions.e: PEA is non-shockable: continue high-quality CPR (30:2) and give adrenaline 1 mg IV as soon as access is obtained, then every 3 to 5 minutes, with no shock.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.

clues: organised complexes at 60 per minute but there is no pulse
No drugs have been given yet
steps.x: Organised rhythm, no pulse: **PEA**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Non-shockable: CPR plus **adrenaline 1 mg immediately**.

elim: In non-shockable rhythms adrenaline is given immediately.
Amiodarone is only for shock-refractory VF/pulseless VT.
No longer used in arrest.
PEA is non-shockable.

steps.x: **A. Continue CPR and give adrenaline 1 mg IV now.** Non-shockable: adrenaline 1 mg ASAP then every 3 to 5 minutes; shockable: after the 3rd shock.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man remains in ventricular fibrillation during a cardiac arrest. He has received five unsynchronised shocks. After the third shock he was given adrenaline 1 mg IV and amiodarone 300 mg IV, and adrenaline has since been repeated. CPR is ongoing.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional drug now?
questions.e: Amiodarone 300 mg is given after the third shock in VF/pulseless VT; a further 150 mg is given if VF persists after five shocks.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.
Still in VF after **5 shocks**, 300 mg amiodarone already given.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Next: **amiodarone 150 mg**.

elim: Not used in cardiac arrest.
The 300 mg dose was given after the 3rd shock; the next dose is 150 mg.
Not used in arrest.
Only for hyperkalaemia or calcium channel blocker overdose.

steps.x: **B. Amiodarone 150 mg IV.** Amiodarone: 300 mg after shock 3, 150 mg after shock 5 (lidocaine is an alternative).

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman who injects drugs has a cardiac arrest in the Emergency Department. CPR is in progress. Two attempts at peripheral IV cannulation have failed because her veins are thrombosed. She is in asystole and needs adrenaline.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate route for drug administration?
questions.e: If IV access fails, arrest drugs are given by the intraosseous route (proximal humerus, proximal tibia or distal tibia).

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.

clues: Two attempts at peripheral IV cannulation have failed
steps.x: IV access has **failed**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Use the **intraosseous** route.

elim: No longer recommended for arrest drugs.
Absorption is unreliable with no circulation.
No absorption without circulation.
Not a route for arrest drugs.

steps.x: **C. Intraosseous.** No IV access in arrest = intraosseous (humerus or tibia).

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman who is 34 weeks pregnant collapses in the antenatal clinic. She is unresponsive and pulseless. CPR has started with her lying flat on her back on a trolley. The obstetric team has been called.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Delay CPR until the obstetrician arrives
Left lateral tilt of about 15 degrees
Place her in the right lateral position
questions.e: In a pregnant woman beyond 20 weeks, the gravid uterus compresses the aorta and IVC; a left lateral tilt of about 15 degrees (or manual uterine displacement) improves venous return during CPR.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.
Over 20 weeks pregnant, **supine**: aortocaval compression.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Left lateral tilt about 15 degrees**.

elim: CPR must not be delayed.
The left side relieves aortocaval compression.
Compressions cannot be given prone.
Does not relieve aortocaval compression.

steps.x: **B. Left lateral tilt of about 15 degrees.** Pregnant over 20 weeks in arrest: left lateral tilt about 15 degrees.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man is stabbed in the right chest. In the Emergency Department he becomes pulseless with PEA. Before arrest his trachea was deviated to the left, breath sounds were absent on the right and his neck veins were distended. CPR is in progress.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Needle decompression in the right 2nd intercostal space
questions.e: Tension pneumothorax (a 4T) is treated immediately with a wide-bore cannula into the 2nd intercostal space (or thoracostomy), not imaging.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.

clues: trachea was deviated to the left
breath sounds were absent on the right
steps.x: Right tension pneumothorax causing PEA.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Decompress the right side now**.

elim: Delays treatment of a clinical diagnosis.
For shock-refractory VF/pulseless VT.
Wrong side; the pneumothorax is on the right.
PEA is non-shockable.

steps.x: **D. Needle decompression in the right 2nd intercostal space.** Tension pneumothorax in arrest: decompress immediately, no X-ray.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman is 6 days after a hysterectomy. She becomes acutely breathless with a swollen right calf and then arrests. The monitor shows PEA. Bedside echo shows a dilated right ventricle with no pericardial fluid. CPR has been ongoing for 10 minutes.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Thrombolysis and continue CPR for 60 to 90 minutes
questions.e: Suspected massive PE in arrest is treated with thrombolysis (for example alteplase), and prolonged CPR of 60 to 90 minutes may be warranted to allow it to work.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.
Post-op DVT, then PEA with a **dilated right ventricle**: massive PE.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Thrombolyse and keep going 60 to 90 minutes**.

elim: No pneumothorax features.
There is no pericardial fluid.
After thrombolysis, CPR should continue for 60 to 90 minutes.
PEA is non-shockable.

steps.x: **D. Thrombolysis and continue CPR for 60 to 90 minutes.** PE arrest: thrombolysis and prolonged CPR (60 to 90 minutes).

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has a VF arrest on the coronary care unit. After two shocks he has return of spontaneous circulation. He is intubated. His pulse rate is 96 bpm, BP 104/68 mmHg and oxygen saturation 90% on the ventilator. His ECG shows an inferior STEMI.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Discharge to the ward once stable
Give amiodarone 300 mg as a further arrest drug
Oxygen, urgent coronary angiography and ICU care
questions.e: Post-ROSC care is oxygen (targeting normal saturations), treating the underlying cause (here PCI for the STEMI) and ICU care.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.
ROSC after VF; hypoxic, and the cause is a **STEMI**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Post-ROSC: **oxygen, treat cause (PCI), ICU**.

elim: Post-ROSC patients need intensive care.
He needs ongoing airway support and ICU care.
He has ROSC; further arrest drugs are not needed.
He has a perfusing rhythm.

steps.x: **D. Oxygen, urgent coronary angiography and ICU care.** After ROSC: oxygen, treat the underlying cause, ICU.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman has a cardiac arrest on a medical ward. CPR is in progress. The defibrillator pads have been attached and the monitor shows ventricular fibrillation. The defibrillator is now charging, which takes about 8 seconds. A student stops compressions and steps back.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate action while the defibrillator charges?
o: Stand clear until the shock is given
questions.e: Compressions continue while the defibrillator charges, to minimise pauses; everyone stands clear only for the shock itself.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.
Defibrillator charging and compressions have stopped.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Keep compressing** while it charges.

elim: She is in VF, so there is no pulse; pausing wastes perfusion time.
Compressions are the priority during charging.
Given after the 3rd shock, not before the first.
Compressions continue until the moment of shocking.

steps.x: **B. Continue chest compressions.** Minimise pauses: compress while charging; stand clear only to shock.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has a witnessed cardiac arrest at home. His wife does not start CPR and the ambulance arrives 12 minutes later. He has ROSC after defibrillation but remains in a coma with signs of severe brain injury. A student asks why the delay was so harmful.
questions.q: Which is the best explanation for his brain injury?
o: Direct electrical injury from the shock
Loss of cerebral perfusion causing hypoxic injury within minutes
questions.e: Cardiac arrest stops cerebral and coronary perfusion immediately; without prompt effective CPR, irreversible hypoxic brain injury begins within minutes. Early compressions matter more than any drug.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the stem.
No CPR for **12 minutes**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: No cerebral perfusion: **hypoxic brain injury within minutes**.

elim: Not the mechanism of post-arrest brain injury.
Defibrillation does not injure the brain.
Not the main mechanism; the brain was globally unperfused.
CPR maintains perfusion; it does not cause the injury.

steps.x: **D. Loss of cerebral perfusion causing hypoxic injury within minutes.** Arrest = no brain perfusion; hypoxic injury starts within minutes, so compress early.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man has a VF arrest on the coronary care unit. A single unsynchronised shock is delivered. The monitor then shows organised narrow complexes preceded by P waves at 80 per minute, and a pulse is felt.
questions.q: Which is the best explanation for the appearance of sinus rhythm?
o: The SA node resumes as pacemaker after the myocardium depolarises together
The shock blocked the AV node
The shock directly stimulated the SA node to fire faster
The shock restored coronary blood flow
questions.e: Defibrillation depolarises a critical mass of myocardium at once, wiping out chaotic VF activity; this allows the SA node to resume as the dominant pacemaker with an organised rhythm.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the stem.
One shock, then **sinus rhythm** with a pulse.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Whole myocardium depolarised, then **SA node takes over**.

elim: No drug has been given.
Blocking the AV node would not restore sinus rhythm.
The shock resets the whole myocardium, not just the SA node.
The shock acts electrically, not on the coronaries.

steps.x: **B. The SA node resumes as pacemaker after the myocardium depolarises together.** Defibrillation resets the myocardium so the SA node can lead again.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man is in cardiac arrest. The monitor shows organised QRS complexes at 70 per minute but no pulse. A foundation doctor asks why the team is not delivering a shock as they did for a patient in VF earlier that day.
questions.q: Which is the best explanation?
o: Electrical activity is organised but produces no mechanical output
PEA is always caused by hypothermia
Shocks are only given in hospital
The heart is already in VF
questions.e: PEA is organised electrical activity that fails to generate a mechanical contraction or pulse, usually from a reversible cause, so defibrillation will not help. The priority is finding the 4H/4T cause.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the stem.

clues: organised QRS complexes at 70 per minute but no pulse
why the team is not delivering a shock
steps.x: Organised complexes, **no output**: PEA.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: There is no chaotic activity for a shock to reset: **organised but no mechanical output**.

elim: Not the reason; a shock simply has nothing to correct.
PEA has many causes (the 4Hs and 4Ts).
Shocks are given wherever the rhythm is shockable.
VF is chaotic, with no organised complexes.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman is in VF arrest that persists after three shocks. Once compressions restart, she is given adrenaline 1 mg and amiodarone 300 mg IV. After the next shock she has ROSC. A student asks how the amiodarone helped.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of action of amiodarone?
o: Blocks muscarinic receptors at the SA node
Increases vagal tone at the AV node
Prolongs the action potential and refractory period
Stimulates beta-1 receptors to increase contractility
questions.e: Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic: it prolongs the cardiac action potential and refractory period, stabilising the myocardium in shock-refractory VF or pulseless VT.
